newsitem.title: USA: Fed may tighten in spring, summer - Bank of America.
newsitem.headline: Fed may tighten in spring, summer - Bank of America.

text.p: Responding to a recent pickup in economic growth, the Federal Reserve may tighten monetary policy this spring, according to John O. Wilson, executive vice president and chief economist at Bank of America.

Wilson said the Fed would hike the federal funds rate a quarter-point, to 5-1/2 percent from 5-1/4 percent. Should economic growth not moderate sufficiently, the Fed may tighten again during the summer, he added.

Writing in the latest edition of the Bank of America's Economic & Business Outlook, Wilson and co-author Frank McCormick, vice president and senior economist at San Francisco-based Bank of America, said economic growth is expected to slow from 2.8 percent in the first quarter of this year to 2.0 percent in the fourth quarter because of increasingly restrictive monetary policy and slightly restrictive fiscal policy.

Regarding tightening by the Fed, the report notes that several members of the Federal Reserve Board have recently indicated that they are now more concerned about rapid economic growth and a pickup of inflation than they were a few months ago.

Furthermore, two members of the Federal Reserve Board who were leaning against tightening monetary policy -- Janet Yellen and Lawrence Lindsey -- have recently resigned. If President Clinton is slow to appoint successors, as he has been in the past, this will tilt the Fed toward a more restrictive monetary policy for the next few meetings, the report said.
The Outlook contains these additional observations by Wilson and McCormick:

-- The yield on 30-year Treasury bonds is expected to edge up to 6.8 percent in the March-to-May period as the Fed tightens, before gradually declining to 6.5 percent in mid-1998 as the economy slows.
-- Consumer inflation will likely remain below 3.0 percent this year and next year, as falling energy prices more than offset the upward pressure on inflation from accelerating wage rates.

The report also discusses President Clinton's proposed fiscal 1998 budget. The budget technically succeeds in reducing the deficit to zero on paper by 2002, according to the report, but it does so only by making assumptions that are more favorable than those of the Congressional Budget Office, the official arbiter of budget balance. Using the CBO's assumptions, Clinton's budget is still about $50 billion in deficit in 2002, the report said.

Even using Clinton's more optimistic assumptions, his proposed budget would result in higher deficits this year and next year -- $126 billion and $121 billion, versus $107 billion last year, the BoA economists said. It is not until 2000 that the deficit would drop below last year's level, to $87 billion.

Moreover, three-fourths of the deficit reduction and two-thirds of the spending cuts would not occur until 2001 and 2002. The President's budget also fails to address the explosion of entitlement spending expected to occur when the baby boomers start to retire early in the next century, the report added.
